Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019. The school offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and offers January enrollment. == History == UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the John Marshall Law School and initially accredited by the American Bar Association in 1951. It merged with the University of Illinois at Chicago in 2019, becoming the University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School. On May 20, 2021, following review by a university task force, the school announced its official change of name to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, effective July 1. The board of trustees acknowledged that "newly discovered research", uncovered by historian Paul Finkelman, had revealed that influential 19th century U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Marshall was a slave trader and owner who practiced "pro-slavery jurisprudence", which was deemed inappropriate for the school's namesake. UIC Law is located in Chicago's central financial and legal district, most commonly known as The Loop. It is across the street from the Dirksen Federal Building, which houses the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit and the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, and about four blocks from the Daley Center, which houses the Circuit Court of Cook County and the Bilandic Building site of the Illinois Appellate Court (First District). The Chicago Bar Association is next door to the law school. URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law

Page Title: University of Illinois Chicago School of Law Content: The University of Illinois Chicago School of Law (UIC Law) is the law school of the University of Illinois Chicago, a public research university in Chicago, Illinois. Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019. The school offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and offers January enrollment. == History == UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the John Marshall Law School and initially accredited by the American Bar Association in 1951. It merged with the University of Illinois at Chicago in 2019, becoming the University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School. On May 20, 2021, following review by a university task force, the school announced its official change of name to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, effective July 1. The board of trustees acknowledged that "newly discovered research", uncovered by historian Paul Finkelman, had revealed that influential 19th century U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Marshall was a slave trader and owner who practiced "pro-slavery jurisprudence", which was deemed inappropriate for the school's namesake. UIC Law is located in Chicago's central financial and legal district, most commonly known as The Loop. It is across the street from the Dirksen Federal Building, which houses the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit and the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, and about four blocks from the Daley Center, which houses the Circuit Court of Cook County and the Bilandic Building site of the Illinois Appellate Court (First District). The Chicago Bar Association is next door to the law school. == Admissions and costs == For the class entering in 2023, UIC Law accepted 69.53% of applicants, with 27.96% of those accepted enrolling. The average enrollee had a 152 LSAT score and 3.39 undergraduate GPA. Tuition and fees at UIC Law for the 2020-2021 academic year is $39,014 for Illinois residents and $48,014 for out of state residents. == Academics == === Curriculum === UIC Law has day and evening divisions, with identical instruction, course content, and scholastic requirements. Lawyering Skills courses, which focus on writing, research, and oral argument, are an integral part of the core curriculum. These courses are taught in small groups, to maximize the individual attention given to each student. A student may earn a J.D. certificate in a certain area of the law or focus more emphatically and earn a joint degree (J.D./LL.M.). The law school also offers Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Jurisprudence (M.J.) programs for practicing attorneys and non-attorney professionals and other individual students. UIC School of Law offers seven Master of Laws (LL.M.) programs for attorneys seeking specialized education in legal issues and for current J.D. students who would like the maximum concentration in particular areas of the law. UIC Law offers a comprehensive curriculum in the following areas: Employee Benefits Law, Estate Planning, Information Technology and Privacy Law, Intellectual Property Law, International Business and Trade Law, Real Estate Law, and Tax Law. === Journals and organizations === There are four honors programs: UIC Law Review, UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law ("RIPL"), the Moot Court Honors Program, and the Trial Advocacy & Dispute Resolution Honors Program. UIC Law sends teams to more than 30 moot court and mock trial competitions annually. The student community at UIC Law includes more than 50 student organizations engaging in social awareness, community service, legal discussions, and social activities. === Clinics === UIC Law students are required to earn three experiential learning credits – working in a clinic, externship, or a combination of both – in order to graduate. The law school offers students practical opportunities through its seven Community Legal Clinics and more than 50 externship placement sites. Clinics include the Community Enterprise & Solidarity Economy Clinic, Fair Housing Legal Support Center & Clinic, International Human Rights Clinic, USPTO-certified IP Patent Clinic, USPTO-certified IP Trademark Clinic, Pro Bono Litigation Clinic, and the Veterans Legal Clinic. Externship opportunities include judicial, governmental, and non-profit placements, as well as a Semester-in-Practice program that allows JD students to earn a semester of credit hours immersed in a legal market outside of Chicago. === Global Legal Skills Conference Series === The Global Legal Skills Conference Series was founded in 2005 as a forum for professors who teach Legal English and international legal skills to exchange information on teaching techniques and materials. The conference connects legal writing professionals and other professors who have an interest in teaching international students and lawyers who speak English as a second language. Since its inception, the Global Legal Skills Conference has been held four times in Chicago, once in Washington, D.C., twice in Mexico, twice in Costa Rica, and twice in Italy. The conference now also includes presentations of GLS Awards for individual achievement, institutional vision, and outstanding publications. == Library == The Louis L. Biro Law Library occupies the 6th – 10th floors of the law school's State Street building. A team of professional librarians and staff members work to serve the students during the 96 hours/week that the library is open. The library holds over 263,003 volumes and microform equivalents and provides on-campus and remote access to some of those titles via their specialty electronic databases. It is continually adding more online subscriptions to its growing collection of electronic resources, including Lexis, Westlaw, CALI Lessons, BNA Premier, IICLE SmartBooks, Max Planck Encyclopedia of Public International Law Online, Justis International Law Reports, Courtroom View Network, which contains audio versions of law school casebooks and streaming trial videos, and Mango languages, an easy to follow system for learning over 20 different languages. Students have wireless access throughout the law school and the library offers seating for 750, including twelve group study rooms. In addition to supporting the research & instructional needs of the students, faculty & staff of the law school, the library is also open to law school alumni and members of the Chicago Bar Association, whose headquarters building is next door. == Bar examination passage == In 2023, the overall bar examination passage rate for the law school's first-time examination takers was 59.19%. The average first-time pass rate for ABA accredited schools was 78.14%. The Ultimate Bar Pass Rate for the school, which the ABA defines as the passage rate for graduates who sat for bar examinations within two years of graduating, was 80.51% for the class of 2021. == Employment == According to the school's official ABA-required disclosures for 2023 graduates, within 10 months after graduation 196 (67.59%) of the 290-member graduating class were employed in full-time positions requiring bar passage (i.e. as attorneys) and 17 (5.86%) were employed in full-time JD advantage positions. Attorney positions were in various size law firms, most in 1–10-attorney firms but some in firms exceeding 500 attorneys; 10 graduates obtained local or state judicial clerkships and four obtained federal clerkships. Seventy-five of the class were otherwise employed in public interest, government, higher education, or business. Seventy-two members (24.83%) were unemployed or employed short–term or part–time. == Rankings and reputation == In the 2024 U.S. News & World Report ranking, the school was ranked 161st in the country out of 196 schools (bottom 18%). == Notable alumni and faculty == == References == == External links == Media related to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law at Wikimedia Commons Official website URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law

May 23, 2021. https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/uic-removes-john-marshalls-name-from-law-school-due-to-slave-ownership/2516781/ - Overview/summary (tertiary; use cautiously) - Wikipedia: University of Illinois Chicago School of Law. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law - Excerpt: “Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019.” and “UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the John Marshall Law School…” Credibility notes: - Primary confirmation of the 2019 merger/affiliation comes from UIC Today (university-hosted). Part 2 — UIC’s official PhD dissertation repositories/entry points, access constraints, and search guidance 1) INDIGO – UIC’s institutional repository (Electronic Theses & Dissertations) - Primary entry point for ETDs: https://indigo.uic.edu/etd - What it is: The official repository where UIC dissertations and theses are deposited and discovered online. - Access constraints (from UIC Library’s official help article): - “Some dissertations and all theses published prior to 2011 are available only in print.” - “Visitors may need to visit the Library to access both electronic and print versions.” - Note: During this session, automated access to https://indigo.uic.edu/ returned 403 Forbidden, which is consistent with repositories restricting automated scraping; the UIC Library help article above provides the official ETD link for human access. - Effective searching: - Use keywords such as author name, title words, program/department, advisor, and topical terms. - Filter/sort by year/date where available; review metadata fields (degree, department) to refine. - If an item is not accessible online, pivot to UIC Library Search (catalog) to locate print holdings. 2) UIC Library help article: “Search for UIC theses and dissertations” - URL: https://library.uic.edu/help-articles/search-for-uic-theses-and-dissertations/ - Why it’s authoritative: Official UIC Library guidance consolidating all primary discovery routes for UIC theses and dissertations. - Key excerpts and guidance: - “To search UIC dissertations and theses online, visit INDIGO, UIC’s institutional repository” (link given to https://indigo.uic.edu/etd). - “You can also use UIC Library Search. Visitors may need to visit the Library to access both electronic and print versions.” - External resources listed include ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global (proxy link below), British Library Research Repository, and Center for Research Libraries. - Effective searching (UIC Library Search at https://library.uic.edu/search): - Select “UIC Catalog Only.” - Filters: Resource type = Dissertations; Library = choose a University Library site. - Add department/program names, advisor names, author names, topical keywords, and date ranges to narrow. 3) UIC Library Collections entry: Theses, Dissertations & UIC Publications - URL: https://library.uic.edu/collections/uic-publications/ - What it is: A collections-level entry point for UIC publications, including theses and dissertations, with links to discovery options and library services. - Access constraints: - Mirrors those noted in the help article (pre-2011 theses generally print only; full text availability varies (embargoes/licensing). - Effective searching: - Use Advanced Search; set University/Institution to “University of Illinois Chicago” to target UIC works. - Filters: Degree (e.g., Ph.D.), Subject/discipline, Date range, Full text. - Combine author, advisor, department/program, and topic keywords for precision. 5) INDIGO submission requirements (context for depositors; informs access/embargo practices) - URL: https://researchguides.uic.edu/indigo/deposit - What it is: UIC Library guidance for authors depositing into INDIGO; helpful context on metadata/embargo that can affect public availability. Practical search strategies across platforms - Keywords to use: author name(s), advisor name(s), program/department (e.g., “Mechanical Engineering,” “Public Health”), specific topic terms, and title phrase fragments. - Filters to apply: - UIC Library Search: UIC Catalog Only; Resource type = Dissertations; Library site; publication date range. - ProQuest: Institution = University of Illinois Chicago; Degree = Ph.D.; Subject; Date range; Full text. - INDIGO ETD: search by author/title/keyword; sort by date; use facets if available (discipline/date). - Troubleshooting/constraints: - Pre-2011 theses may be print-only; use the catalog to get call numbers and locations and plan on-site access if you are a visitor. - Off-campus access to ProQuest requires UIC authentication via the proxy link. - Some recent ETDs may be under embargo; if access is restricted, consult the catalog, request assistance from a librarian, or consider interlibrary loan options. Visitors may need to visit the Library to access both electronic and print versions.” URL: https://library.uic.edu/help-articles/search-for-uic-theses-and-dissertations/ - ProQuest proxied link (institutional access): http://proxy.cc.uic.edu/login?url=http://search.proquest.com/dissertations/advanced?accountid=14552 Conclusion - The university is the University of Illinois Chicago (UIC), which merged with The John Marshall Law School (founded 1899; named after Chief Justice John Marshall) in 2019. Authoritative confirmations are provided via UIC Today (official university communications) and corroborated by reputable media. - UIC’s official dissertation entry points include INDIGO (ETD collection), the UIC Library help article (with catalog search guidance and access constraints), the UIC Library Collections page for UIC publications, and institutional access to ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global. Goal: Identify ALL plausible UIC PhD dissertations that investigate the physical mechanisms of filtration in coalescing filters focusing on airborne liquid drops (aerosol droplets) during separation processes, and extract the advisor’s full name(s). Provide comprehensive evidence (URLs, metadata fields, quotes/snippets), verify scope (airborne/aerosol vs. liquid–liquid coalescers), and note uncertainties.

Context:
- University is University of Illinois Chicago (UIC). We must target UIC’s PhD dissertations in the official repositories or discovery platforms (INDIGO ETD, UIC Library Search, ProQuest public metadata), and broader web if needed.
- Topic keywords/synonyms include: “coalescing filter”, “coalescence filter”, “coalescer”, “fibrous coalescing filter”, “mist filter”, “demister”, “liquid aerosol”, “aerosol droplet”, “airborne liquid drops”, “droplet coalescence”, “separation process(es)”, “filtration mechanisms”. Exclude liquid–liquid coalescers used in emulsions unless the context explicitly involves airborne droplets.

Tasks:
1) Search within UIC INDIGO ETD (https://indigo.uic.edu/etd if accessible) for the above keywords. If INDIGO is blocked or inaccessible, use Google/Bing queries like: site:indigo.uic.edu coalesc* filter aerosol; site:indigo.uic.edu dissertation coalescing filter; site:indigo.uic.edu “mist filter” or “demister” or “liquid aerosol”. 
2) Use UIC Library Search (https://library.uic.edu/search) with filters: UIC Catalog Only; Resource type = Dissertations (and/or Theses) to find UIC PhD records with those keywords in title/abstract/subject. 
3) Use ProQuest Dissertations & Theses (public side, no login) to search for institution = University of Illinois at Chicago (or University of Illinois Chicago) and keywords listed above. Even if full text is gated, advisor names often appear in public metadata. 
4) Also try Google Scholar or general Google web search combining the keywords with site restrictions (site:uic.edu, site:indigo.uic.edu) and with phrases like “PhD dissertation” or “doctoral dissertation”. 
5) For each plausible candidate, confirm it truly studies airborne droplets in coalescing/fibrous filters (not oil–water coalescers). Capture: title, author, year, department/degree, abstract snippet (relevant lines), repository/catalog page URL, and PDF URL if available.
6) Extract the advisor’s full name. Preferred order of sources: (a) explicit Advisor/Committee Chair field in INDIGO metadata; (b) the dissertation PDF front matter (title page or committee approval page) where full names typically appear; (c) ProQuest metadata Advisor field; (d) UIC catalog record if it lists advisors. If multiple advisors/co-advisors are listed, capture each with labels. Avoid abbreviated initials when a fuller name is available; if only initials appear, note the limitation and attempt to corroborate from another source/PDF.
7) For near-miss items (e.g., liquid–liquid coalescers or non-UIC), list them under “excluded/near-misses” with brief reasons for exclusion.

Deliverable:
- A structured report with sections: (A) Candidates found (each with title, author, year, department/degree, scope verification, advisor full name(s) with evidence quotes and links); (B) Excluded/near-misses with reasons; (C) Any remaining uncertainties or discrepancies (e.g., differing advisor listings across sources, embargoed PDFs); and (D) Recommendations for any follow-up retrieval steps if needed (e.g., on-campus catalog/PDF access).

Notes:
- Prioritize advisor full names as written in the official record/PDF. If the repository page omits the advisor but the PDF includes it on the approval page, quote the exact line(s). If the PDF is scan-only, transcribe carefully.
- Include all plausible candidates; do not prematurely filter to one. Provide enough detail to judge alignment with the described topic (airborne liquid drops and coalescing filtration mechanisms).

Some features of this site may not work without it. ## Fluid Mechanics of Nano-textured Coalescing Filters ![Thumbnail]() ##### View/Open [Sahu\_Rakesh.pdf (7.349Mb)](/web/20191121231939/https%3A//indigo.uic.edu/bitstream/handle/10027/19349/Sahu_Rakesh.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y) ##### Date 2015-02-27 ##### Author Sahu, Rakesh P. ##### Metadata [Show full item record](/web/20191121231939/https%3A//indigo.uic.edu/handle/10027/19349?show=full) ##### Abstract The work deals with the different stages of filtration within the coalescing filters on the physical level. The main stages involved in separation of airborne liquid drops brought by a gas flux onto a coalescing filter were separated into several fundamental problems studied experimentally and theoretically. Novel experimental setups were designed for conducting the experiments and theoretical modeling was used to explain, rationalize and predict the observations. The effect of static wettability under dynamic drop impact was found to be negligible after the drop crosses a certain threshold velocity. The hydrodynamic focusing of the liquid drop into the pores of the membrane overcomes the static wettability. It has been shown that the superhydrophobicity does not prevent water from being delivered into a filter if the impact velocity surpasses a threshold value of the order of 3 m/s, and the hydrodynamic focusing becomes important. As the liquid drops get inside the filter, it gets intercepted with the fiber matrix inside. As the air keeps blowing the intercepted liquid drops move over the fibers in different directions depending on the direction of air blowing with respect to the fiber axis. The different breakup modes observed during cross blowing was mapped onto the We-Oh plane. Drop hopping between the fibers was also observed. Liquid drops were observed to reach a significant depth of its thickness due to the hydrodynamic focusing. In addition, propagation of liquid fronts associated with drop boundaries inside non-wettable nonwovens was studied experimentally and theoretically, as well as the entrainment of nanoparticles by such fronts. As the usage of nanofibers is steadily increasing in the filtration industry, the mechanically-driven rearrangement of nanofiber membranes under the action of drop evaporation at the front surface becomes very important. The formation of big holes on the suspended nanofiber mat is addressed in the experiments of the present work. Void formation was uncovered and quantitatively described. The findings of the present work reported are useful for development of novel coalescing filters and proper understanding of their operation. ##### Subject Nanofibers Drop Impact Drop Penetration Drop Blowing Drop Evaporation Drop Coalescence ##### Type thesis text ##### Date available in INDIGO 2015-02-27T21:43:57Z ##### URI [http://hdl.handle.net/10027/19349](http://web.archive.org/web/20191121231939/http%3A//hdl.handle.net/10027/19349) ##### Collections * [UIC Dissertations and Theses](/web/20191121231939/https%3A//indigo.uic.edu/handle/10027/8766) --- [DSpace software](http://web.archive.org/web/20191121231939/http%3A//www.dspace.org/) copyright © 2002-2015 [DuraSpace](http://web.archive.org/web/20191121231939/http%3A//www.duraspace.org/) [Contact Us](/web/20191121231939/https%3A//indigo.uic.edu/contact) | [Send Feedback](/web/20191121231939/https%3A//indigo.uic.edu/feedback) | [Privacy Statement](http://web.archive.org/web/20191121231939/https%3A//www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/web_privacy) Theme by [![Atmire NV](/web/20191121231939im_/https://indigo.uic.edu/themes/Mirage2/images/@mirelogo-small.png)](http://web.archive.org/web/20191121231939/http%3A//atmire.com/ "Atmire NV") SearchSearch Search INDIGO This Collection ##
